title: Polynomial-time computation of addition-chain length
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given an integer \(n\ge 1\) in binary, outputs its exact shortest addition-chain length \(\ell\)\((n)\) in time polynomial in the binary input length?
definitions: An addition chain for n is a strictly increasing sequence of integers \(1=a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots <a_{r}=n\) such that, for every \(i\ge 1\), there are \(j,k<i\) with \(a_{i}=a_{j}+a_{k}; j=k\) is allowed. Its length is r, the number of additions, so \(\ell\)\((1)=0\). The input is the ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, of length \(b=\lfloor \log _{2}n\rfloor +1\). The output is \(\ell\)\((n)\) in binary. One fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine must halt within \(p(b)\) steps on every input, for one fixed polynomial p. All bit operations and output writing count. Subtraction, arbitrary constants other than the initial 1, and multiplication of previously formed exponents are not allowed chain operations. Chain entries can be reused arbitrarily. The cost of finding \(\ell\)\((n)\) is distinct from the number \(\ell\)\((n)\) of steps in the chain itself.
answer_criterion: Give such an exact algorithm with one polynomial bound, or prove that no such algorithm exists. An approximation to \(\ell\)\((n), a\) fast heuristic, polynomial time in n rather than log n, or exact results for a restricted family of exponents do not resolve the question. NP-hardness of a multiple-target variant does not establish hardness for this single-target problem. Conditional hardness must retain its assumption.

context_blocks.text: Exponentiation can reuse powers: multiplying aʲ and \(a^{k}\) produces \(a^{j+k}\). Thus a chain specifies a multiplication-only program for an arbitrary formal power \(a^{n}\). Erickson’s notes explain why repeated squaring uses \(O(\log  n)\) multiplications and then ask whether the absolute minimum count can be computed efficiently.

For example, 1,2,3,5,10,15 gives five multiplications for \(a^{15}\). A convenient repeated-squaring implementation can use six. This small difference illustrates the exact optimization target: the asymptotic order of the chain length is already understood, while selecting its optimal integer value can require much more search.

Each chain step can at most double its largest entry, giving \(\ell\)\((n)\ge \lceil \log _{2}n\rceil\). Reading the binary digits of n gives a chain with at most \(2\lfloor \log _{2}n\rfloor\) steps. Consequently a shortest chain has \(O(b)\) entries of at most b bits. Exhaustive enumeration is finite and yields an exact algorithm, but not a polynomial bound in b.

The decision problem “\(\ell\)\((n)\le k\)?” is in NP: a short chain, together with its predecessor indices, is a polynomial-size certificate. Computing the exact length is equivalent to deciding these thresholds in polynomial time, by searching between the elementary bounds. This observation does not establish NP-completeness.

Koziel and coauthors explicitly distinguish the single-target problem from the generalized task of forming several specified values, for which NP-completeness is known. Their work develops efficient chains for cryptographic arithmetic. The 2025 primary article by Kempes and coauthors likewise describes the exact complexity of the single-target problem as unknown.

The Scholz–Brauer conjecture already appears as TCS-7170. It bounds \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)\) in terms of \(\ell\)\((n)\); even its resolution would not supply a polynomial-time method for finding \(\ell\)\((n)\) on arbitrary binary input. The present algorithmic question has a different conclusion and computational significance.

why: Locate the exact computational difficulty of optimizing multiplication-only exponentiation, a basic reusable arithmetic program with short certificates but no known efficient exact optimizer.

importance.reason: A longstanding exact optimization problem at the intersection of arithmetic algorithms, circuit reuse and cryptographic exponentiation. Its single-target complexity is repeatedly distinguished from the solved hardness of the generalized problem; it is not a numerical special case of Scholz–Brauer.

status_note: The single-target polynomial-time question remains unresolved in the checked sources through 11 September 2026. The review does not accept claims of NP-completeness that merely cite the generalized multiple-target theorem.
review_note: The source asks for the minimum number, so this card asks to compute the length, not a stronger unproved search-to-length equivalence. The binary input model and chain operations are specified. Existing TCS-7170 has a distinct structural target.
